Chapter 6: Feedback Loops—When Algorithms Reinforce Their Own Mistakes
Have you ever noticed how sometimes, life feels like it’s running on autopilot? Invisible hands seem to nudge us in directions we never really chose.
In the world of big data, those nudges become something trickier—feedback loops that quietly reinforce the very problems algorithms are supposed to fix.
Let me paint you a picture. Imagine a city where schools are graded by test scores. The lowest scoring schools? They lose funding. Suddenly, it’s harder for them to attract talented teachers or offer after-school programs. As their resources shrink, test scores drop even further, and the cycle just tightens.
Think about a bright student who’s struggling. Their school library is closed, after-school help gets canceled, and the model that was designed to reward improvement actually ends up punishing the kids who need help the most.
Now, in another part of that same city, police patrols are guided by predictive software. The algorithm uses years of old arrest data to determine where officers should go. So, they’re sent to the same neighborhoods again and again. Every new arrest—no matter how minor—simply confirms the model’s belief that this is a “problem area.”
Residents start feeling watched. A teenager, stopped on his way home, can’t help but wonder why he’s always under suspicion. And so, the cycle continues: more patrols, more arrests, more data feeding the same bias.
Here’s something important: these feedback loops aren’t usually intentional. They happen because algorithms are built to learn from the past. But if the past is shaped by inequality, the predictions just keep repeating that history.
Picture a hiring algorithm. It might notice that certain resumes tend to get hired—because those candidates got the job before. Over time, it focuses more and more on those patterns, overlooking anyone who doesn’t quite fit the mold.
For the people caught inside these loops, it’s pretty stifling. A teacher who works day and night for her students feels invisible—reduced to a set of numbers. A job seeker, facing rejection after rejection, starts to believe it’s their fault, instead of realizing the model is stacked against them.
It becomes clear: feedback loops aren’t just bugs in the system. They’re deeper, structural problems that can lock people into disadvantage. Breaking the cycle will take more than just tweaking a few lines of code. It means stepping back and asking tough questions about the data, the assumptions, and the goals behind these systems.
But there’s hope. Some communities are pushing back. Parents are speaking up, demanding that school evaluations look beyond just test scores. Activists are calling for transparency in how policing algorithms are used, making sure communities have a real voice in the process.
These efforts remind us of something powerful: algorithms are not destiny. They’re tools—and like any tool, they can be changed.
So, here’s the key takeaway. If we leave algorithms unchecked, they can make existing problems even worse. But with awareness and a willingness to act, we really can break the cycle and build systems that are fair and truly serve everyone.
